summary: Discusses requirements and design considerations for addressing maintenance points (MIPs) on incoming and outgoing interfaces of nodes in MPLS-TP OAM, including restrictions on how OAM messages must be formed so they reach the right MIP through the forwarding engine. The aim is to make sure OAM messages can be forwarded correctly to the intended point.

eli5.summary: When checking a building, you must name which door you want to inspect. This explains how to name each door.

subtitle: Guidelines for addressing maintenance checkpoints on network interfaces in carrier-grade MPLS.

tldr.problem: MPLS Transport Profile networks need to perform maintenance and troubleshooting at fine-grained points along a path, including separate checkpoints on the incoming and outgoing sides of each router. However, there was no standardized way to address and target these individual checkpoints.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7054 specifies design requirements and restrictions that any addressing mechanism must follow to correctly target per-interface maintenance points while ensuring OAM messages pass through the network's forwarding engine exactly like regular data packets.
tldr.outcome: Operators gain the ability to perform connectivity verification, loopback testing, and performance monitoring with precise fault localization within the network, helping diagnose whether problems are on links between nodes or within specific routers.

today: RFC 7054 is an Informational RFC that provides design guidance for MPLS-TP implementations. Per-interface MIPs have been incorporated into carrier-grade MPLS-TP deployments to enable operators to perform precise fault localization. The RFC does not define a specific addressing mechanism but rather establishes the requirements that any such mechanism must satisfy.

sections.title: MPLS Operations and Maintenance Checkpoints
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) is a version of MPLS designed for carrier-grade transport networks. Like all networks, MPLS-TP requires Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) capabilities to detect and diagnose faults.

OAM functions include connectivity verification, traceroute, loopback testing, and performance monitoring. These operations need to check status at various points along a Label Switched Path (LSP) or Pseudowire (PW). Maintenance Entity Group Intermediate Points (MIPs) are the checkpoints placed at these locations.

Historically, one MIP was placed somewhere inside each node (per-node model). However, to enable more precise fault localization, RFC 6371 defines the concept of per-interface MIPs: multiple MIPs per node, placed on the incoming interface (before the forwarding engine) and outgoing interface (after the forwarding engine). This document elaborates on the requirements and design considerations for addressing these per-interface MIPs.
sections.eli5: MPLS-TP is used by telephone and cable companies for important networks. OAM is the testing and troubleshooting system. MIPs are the checkpoints where you can test. The old way put one checkpoint per router; the new way puts one on each side of the router's forwarding engine to find problems more precisely.

sections.title: The Addressing Problem
sections.content:
OAM messages travel through the network using standard packet mechanisms. For messages targeting a transit point (MIP), the mechanism is the expiration of the MPLS Time-to-Live (TTL) field. For endpoint messages, they are simply delivered as normal. The content of OAM messages is distinguished from data using a Generic Associated Channel Label (GAL) in LSPs or a PW Associated Channel Header (PWACH) in Pseudowires.

However, when multiple MIPs exist on a single node, these mechanisms provide no way to address one particular MIP out of the set. If an OAM message arrives at a node with per-interface MIPs and says "check the connectivity here," which MIP should handle it—the incoming one or the outgoing one?

Any mechanism to solve this must work within the existing OAM framework and be standardized so that different vendors' equipment can interoperate correctly.
sections.eli5: The old OAM system had no way to say "the incoming checkpoint, not the outgoing one." Without standardized labels, different companies would invent different ways to address them, and the equipment wouldn't talk to each other.

sections.title: Per-Node vs Per-Interface OAM Models
sections.content:
In the per-node model, there is one unspecified MIP per node. All OAM requests to that node target the same location. This simplifies implementation but limits fault localization. If a link works fine to the node but client data stops flowing, the fault could be in the node's forwarding engine, on the outgoing interface, or beyond.

In the per-interface model, there are two (or more) MIPs per node: an in-MIP on the incoming interface (before the forwarding engine) and an out-MIP on the outgoing interface (after the forwarding engine). This enables much finer-grained fault localization.

For example, if incoming connectivity tests pass but outgoing tests fail, you know the problem is in the forwarding engine. If connectivity to the outgoing interface of one node fails but the incoming interface of the next node works, the problem is definitely on the link between them. Per-interface MIPs enable operators to quickly narrow down exactly where a fault exists.
sections.eli5: The old system: one checkpoint per box. You test it and know something between here and the next box is broken, but not what. The new system: two checkpoints per box (before and after the forwarding engine). Now you know if it's on the link, in the box, or beyond the box.

sections.title: Design Requirements for MIP Addressing
sections.content:
Any solution for delivering OAM messages to in-MIPs and out-MIPs must satisfy several critical design requirements:

Correct delivery to the right node and right MIP: OAM messages must reach the correct MPLS-TP node and the correct MIP within that node.

Forward OAM packets exactly like data: This is vital. OAM messages intended for an out-MIP must travel through the forwarding engine normally, as if they were regular data packets. If OAM messages destined for out-MIPs are intercepted at the in-MIP and forwarded via some internal messaging system, certain OAM functions fail—specifically loopback, connectivity verification, LSP tracing, and performance measurement all require the OAM message to transit the actual forwarding engine.

Minimize packet inspection overhead: Because OAM packets targeting out-MIPs must be forwarded through the forwarding engine, and because some OAM functions like loopback operate at line rate, the processing overhead for determining whether to process a packet at the in-MIP or forward it must be minimal.

Handle implementation variations: Some existing MPLS-TP nodes implement all queuing and forwarding at the incoming interface; there is no real outgoing interface to attach a MIP to. Solutions must not cause problems with these implementations (such as OAM packets with TTL=0 leaking out).

Support point-to-multipoint: OAM must work correctly on P2MP nodes that have multiple outgoing interfaces, allowing targeting of individual out-MIPs or all out-MIPs at once.
sections.eli5: The addressing mechanism must: (1) get the right test to the right checkpoint, (2) send out-MIP tests through the forwarding engine like normal data, (3) not slow down the network with extra checking, (4) not break older routers, and (5) work on multicast paths.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations and Safety
sections.content:
Although the message format and addressing mechanism must be standardized, much of the per-interface MIP implementation is local to individual nodes. However, standardization ensures that:

Senders can target correctly: A Maintenance Entity Group End Point (MEP) can correctly address an out-MIP of a specific MPLS-TP node, even when that upstream node might be an older implementation without out-MIPs.

Filtering provides safety: If an OAM message intended for a neighboring node's out-MIP leaks beyond its intended scope (because the neighbor is an old implementation that doesn't have out-MIPs), the downstream node can correctly filter it out rather than processing it incorrectly.

Mixing per-node and per-interface OAM on a single node is not recommended, as it can result in OAM message leakage where messages reach unintended MIPs.

Security for OAM is covered in RFC 6371 and RFC 6941. OAM can be used to detect attacks but can also be misused for information gathering or denial-of-service; therefore, implementations must provide security mechanisms and deployments should follow the guidance in those RFCs.
sections.eli5: Different routers might use different versions of per-interface MIPs. The solution must be flexible enough to work with new and old equipment, with safety filters to prevent test messages from going to the wrong place.
